handback.t:
W2 round 1 result: negative on all three questions. Nothing is accepted, and nothing I built beats the best fair baseline on held-out seeds 31-60 under Holm.

`cargo test --release --lib` is green: 110 passed, 0 failed, including 4 new tests of mine.

**Protocol.** I tuned on seeds 1-8 only and evaluated on held-out seeds 31-60 with paired 95% t-CIs and Holm correction. The baselines were keyword, eps-greedy, pooled-ts, hebbian-robust and warm(hebbian-robust). I added two stronger controls of my own to the baseline pool: hebbian re-tuned in my world, and the same learner with edges switched off. In every cell the best fair baseline was warm(hebbian-robust), except overall success in no-traps, where it was keyword.

## 1. Sequential hand-off edges (own world in `w2_workflow`, sim.rs not used)

**World.**
- 6 agents, 8 step types, 3-step workflows, 2000 steps per run.
- A hidden hand-off matrix H[prev][next] changes the success probability: one good next agent (+mag) and one bad (-0.8 mag) per previous agent.
- Routers see only the current step's noisy keywords, plus the previous agent for the edge candidates.
- Three worlds: main (mag .30), weak (.10) and none (0, a null world).
- 5 candidates, each in 3 worlds on 2 metrics (full run and first 501 steps), gave 30 tests in the Holm family.

**Candidates.**
- `seq-edges-dense` and `seq-edges-sparse` (top-k per source): hebbian leader plus directed prev-to-next edges.
- `hebbian+prev-feature`: the obvious control, adding "prev=x" as one more feature. A feature-augmented hebbian is mathematically the same thing as an edge bias, so the novel part is small.
- `seq-add+edges` and `warm(seq-add+edges)`: a joint delta-rule model, v[feature][agent] + g[prev][agent].

**Result: 0 of 30 tests beat the best fair baseline. Every candidate is below warm(hebbian-robust), often by a lot.**

Main world, mean difference versus warm(hebbian-robust), full run / early (all CIs are 95%, 30 seeds):

| Candidate | Full | Early | Seed wins (full) | Holm p (full / early) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| seq-edges-dense | -0.0177 [-0.0324, -0.0031] | -0.0154 [-0.0349, +0.0040] | 10/30 | 0.057 / 0.115 (n.s.) |
| seq-edges-sparse | -0.0282 | -0.0220 | 5/30 | 0.0002 / 0.069 |
| hebbian+prev-feature | -0.0364 | -0.0593 | 2/30 | <1e-4 |
| seq-add+edges | -0.0226 | -0.0471 | 5/30 | 0.0008 / <1e-4 |
| warm(seq-add+edges) | -0.0276 | -0.0495 | 1/30 | <1e-4 |

- Absolute main-world full-run means: warm(hebbian-robust) 0.7739, seq-edges-dense 0.7562, plain hebbian-tuned-here 0.7602. The greedy-given-prev oracle reaches 0.8407, so there is headroom the edges did not capture.
- In the weak and none worlds every candidate is significantly worse (Holm p ≤ 0.012). The best of them, seq-edges-dense, trails by 0.0175 in weak and 0.0306 in none (full run).
- The edge layer costs even in the null world, where there is nothing to learn.
- Edge ablation, main world only: `seq-add+edges` beats the same learner without edges by +0.0150 full [+0.0053, +0.0246] and +0.0207 early, 21/30 wins. These CIs are unadjusted.
- The un-warmed ablation learner is itself weak (0.7364 full), so that gain does not close the gap to warm(hebbian-robust). In the weak world the ablation difference is about 0 (+0.0008).
- `seq-edges-dense` beats the plain prev-feature control by +0.019 full / +0.044 early (unadjusted CIs exclude 0), but both lose to warm(hebbian-robust).

**Memory (sparse edges).** Measured with the `memory_scaling` function in `w2_workflow`, k=4, 20 hand-offs per agent:

| Agents | Dense bytes | Sparse bytes | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 288 | 432 | 0.7x (sparse is larger) |
| 50 | 20,000 | 3,600 | 5.6x |
| 500 | 2,000,000 | 36,000 | 56x |
| 5,000 | 200,000,000 | 360,000 | 556x |

Sparse saves memory at 50+ agents. Behaviour is the cost: the tuned sparse k=1 trailed dense by 0.0105 full in the main world, unadjusted. I did not run a Holm-tested non-inferiority comparison of sparse against dense.

## 2. Faster bench/recover (`w2_fault`, sim.rs read-only)

I added an opt-in `FaultConfig` in `mesh.rs` with `NeuralMesh::with_fault`. It has a failure-streak bench, probation retry backoff, and tuned health knobs. The default is off and unchanged. Metrics are expected success of the routed agent, in failure windows and overall, over 4 scenarios (fixed, random, no-synergy, no-traps), all with team_size 1.

- **The tuner chose no streak-bench.** It picked retry_every 10 with backoff 2 and left the health threshold (0.3) and alpha (0.2) at their defaults.
- **Streak-bench alone (streak 2) is harmful.** It scores about 0.55 overall versus about 0.76, and it benches healthy agents after two unlucky failures.
- **0 of 32 tests beat the best fair baseline, and 0 of 24 beat mesh-robust, under Holm.**
- The best result, `fault-tuned` versus mesh-robust in the fixed scenario, is +0.0109 failure-window [+0.0022, +0.0195] (18/30 wins), but Holm p=0.25. Overall success moved -0.005 to +0.002 (n.s.).
- Versus warm(hebbian-robust), `fault-tuned` is +0.0025 [-0.0116, +0.0166] in the fixed-scenario failure window, n.s. Overall it is -0.0152 [-0.0262, -0.0043], Holm p=0.14.
- `retry5+backoff2-only` is flat (≤ ±0.004, n.s. against mesh-robust).
- In no-traps, mesh-robust and fault-tuned are both significantly worse than keyword on overall success (Holm p<1e-4), a gap that was already there.
- Why the ceiling is low: a failure window costs only about 5 of ~200 task slots with the current EMA bench, so there is almost nothing left for faster benching to recover.

## Files changed

- `src/mesh.rs`: `FaultConfig`, the `fault`, `fail_streak`, `retry_mult` and `probation` fields (all `#[serde(default)]`), `with_fault`, and 2 tests.
- `src/variants.rs`: `SeqEdges`, `SeqEdgesConfig`, `SeqMesh`, `SeqAddRouter`, `SeqAddConfig`, and 2 tests.
- `src/bin/w2_workflow.rs` and `src/bin/w2_fault.rs`: new.
- Results: `results/w2_workflow.json` and `results/w2_fault.json`. Both json files are stale: they come from the first-round runs and do not include the SeqAdd candidates or the ablation baselines. The full second-run output is only in `/tmp/w2_wf2.out`; re-run to regenerate the json.

No other file was touched and there are no commits.

## Reproduce

Build and run from `C:\Users\mariu\neural-mesh` with the toolchain exports and `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=C:/Users/mariu/nm-target-w2`:

- `cargo run --release --bin w2_workflow`
- `cargo run --release --bin w2_fault`

## Verdict

- Sequential edges are rejected: they lose to the router alone, mostly because the reward signal is too noisy for an edge layer to pay off at 2000 steps.
- Fast-bench variants are rejected: no Holm-significant gain, and the streak variant is harmful.
- Sparse edges are a memory saving only at 50+ agents; I never measured a loss-free tradeoff.
- Next steps if wanted: much longer workflows, a real warm start for the edge layer, or a larger agent pool, where edge sparsity and learning actually matter.
